Searching for five recent, well-sourced insights that don't overlap the excluded list.


### Insight 1: Honeycomb sail survives laser push
- **In short:** Engineers built a laser sail lighter than printer paper that reflects most of the beam and barely absorbs heat—the combo starship sails needed but never had together.
- **How it works:**
  - Prototypes weigh under 1 gram per square meter, reflect over 50% of light near a 1.2 micrometer laser band, and absorb under 4%.
  - Alumina face sheets wrap a molybdenum disulfide core, and hexagonal corrugations stiffen the sheet like cardboard without adding much mass.
  - Models suggest optimized versions could reach about 26% of light speed—above the Breakthrough Starshot 20% target—because low absorption stops the sail from melting first.
- **Proof:**
  - [Experimental demonstration of corrugated nanolaminate films as reflective light sails](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41467-026-73414-4)
  - [Experimental demonstration of corrugated nanolaminate films as reflective light sails (arXiv)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2508.05035)
- **Easy to miss because:** Interstellar sail talk still sounds like pure theory, not a film you can hold that already passes the hard optical and weight tests.
- **Image:** https://media.springernature.com/full/springer-static/image/art%3A10.1038%2Fs41467-026-73414-4/MediaObjects/41467_2026_73414_Fig1_HTML.png

### Insight 2: Six thousand atoms stay quantum twelve seconds
- **In short:** A grid of more than 6,100 laser-trapped cesium atoms now keeps quantum memory for 12.6 seconds—while scaling up, not shrinking down.
- **How it works:**
  - About 12,000 optical tweezers hold 6,100 atoms in a room-temperature vacuum setup with trap lifetimes near 23 minutes.
  - Dynamical decoupling pulse trains stretch hyperfine qubit coherence to 12.6 seconds, roughly ten times prior tweezer-array records.
  - Single-qubit gates hit 99.9834% fidelity, and atoms can be moved hundreds of micrometers without wrecking coherence—steps toward error correction at thousands of qubits.
- **Proof:**
  - [A tweezer array with 6,100 highly coherent atomic qubits](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41586-025-09641-4)
  - [A tweezer array with 6,100 highly coherent atomic qubits (PMC)](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12589140/)
- **Easy to miss because:** Bigger quantum machines are usually assumed to get noisier; here coherence got longer as the array grew.
- **Image:** https://data.caltech.edu/records/4m9sp-yzr58/files/single_shot_image.png

### Insight 3: Cancer glue turns mutant RAS off
- **In short:** Drugs once sold as “blockers” can also teach broken cancer RAS proteins to chew up their own fuel molecule GTP—something forty years of drug hunting failed to do.
- **How it works:**
  - Tri-complex inhibitors act as molecular glues that drag cyclophilin A onto active, GTP-loaded mutant RAS.
  - The glued complex reshapes switch-II residues so a water molecule can attack the phosphate—restoring hydrolysis without the usual GAP “arginine finger.”
  - Gly12 mutants gain the most GTPase boost, and those tumors respond more strongly—linking “turn the enzyme back on” to killing power.
- **Proof:**
  - [Pharmacological restoration of GTP hydrolysis by mutant RAS](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41586-024-08283-2)
  - [Crystal structure of KRAS G12D with CYPA and RMC-7977 (PDB 9bgh)](https://pdbj.org/mine/summary/9bgh)
- **Easy to miss because:** RAS cancer drugs are framed as handcuffs on signaling, not as pills that reboot the protein’s built-in off switch.
- **Image:** https://cdn.rcsb.org/images/structures/9bgh_assembly-1.jpeg

### Insight 4: Gut bacterium escorts dendritic cells upward
- **In short:** A newly named gut bug from PD-1 responders can wake immune dendritic cells in the intestine—and those same cells later show up in tumors to arm killer T cells.
- **How it works:**
  - Strain YB328, from the genus *Hominenteromicrobium*, pushes gut dendritic cells toward a CD103⁺CD11b⁻ state through TLR–MyD88, S6K, STAT3, and IRF8.
  - After meeting the bacterium in the gut, those dendritic cells migrate to tumor-draining lymph nodes and the tumor itself.
  - Adding YB328 to fecal transplants from non-responders still boosts anti-PD-1 therapy—suggesting one dominant microbe can override a failing community.
- **Proof:**
  - [Microbiota-driven antitumour immunity mediated by dendritic cell migration](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41586-025-09249-8)
  - [Microbiota-driven antitumour immunity mediated by dendritic cell migration (PubMed)](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/40659786/)
- **Easy to miss because:** Microbiome hype focuses on vague “good bugs,” not a postal route where gut-trained dendritic cells commute to distant tumors.
- **Image:** https://media.springernature.com/full/springer-static/image/art%3A10.1038%2Fs41586-025-09249-8/MediaObjects/41586_2025_9249_Fig1_HTML.png

### Insight 5: Silver rings spin without light push
- **In short:** Three or more silver nanoparticles locked in a curved laser ring can crawl around it together—even when the light carries no steering gradient.
- **How it works:**
  - Identical nanoparticles in a bent optical trap break mirror symmetry, creating many-body electrodynamic forces that are not equal and opposite.
  - A ring of optically bound particles rotates collectively, and the spin direction flips when you reverse the circular polarization handedness.
  - Total sideways force grows with particle count—simulations show roughly forty times the trimer force for 28 particles—without the usual spin-to-orbit light trick.
- **Proof:**
  - [Symmetry breaking-induced N-body electrodynamic forces in optical matter systems](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41467-025-61616-1)
  - [Symmetry breaking-induced N-body electrodynamic forces in optical matter systems (DOI landing)](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41467-025-61616-1)
- **Easy to miss because:** Optical tweezers are taught as passive traps; here the particles’ own collective light scattering becomes a motor.
- **Image:** https://media.springernature.com/full/springer-static/image/art%3A10.1038%2Fs41467-025-61616-1/MediaObjects/41467_2025_61616_Fig1_HTML.png

Searching for recent, cross-verifiable developments not covered in the prior insight list.


### Insight 1: Bile acid grabs a hidden receptor
- **In short:** A gut bile acid that rises during calorie restriction now has a named receiver—TULP3—and that switch can mimic fasting’s anti-aging effects in muscles, worms, and flies.
- **How it works:**
  - Lithocholic acid binds TULP3, which wakes sirtuin enzymes that strip acetyl tags off three spots on the lysosome pump subunit V1E1.
  - That pump slowdown triggers AMPK—the cell’s main energy gauge—through the lysosomal glucose-sensing route.
  - A muscle-only V1E1 mutant mimicking the deacetylated state rejuvenated aged mouse muscle without adding the bile acid itself.
- **Proof:**
  - [Lithocholic acid binds TULP3 to activate sirtuins and AMPK to slow down ageing | Nature](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41586-024-08348-2)
  - [Lithocholic acid phenocopies anti-ageing effects of calorie restriction | Nature](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41586-024-08329-5)
- **Easy to miss because:** Calorie-restriction stories still treat “eat less” as one vague switch—not a bile-acid → TULP3 → v-ATPase → AMPK chain you can trip with chemistry.
- **Image:** https://media.springernature.com/full/springer-static/image/art%3A10.1038%2Fs41586-024-08348-2/MediaObjects/41586_2024_8348_Fig1_HTML.png

### Insight 2: Cell skeleton learns without neurons
- **In short:** A computer model of the actin–myosin cell skeleton can learn input–output force rules the same way contrastive AI does—using force-sensitive proteins and motors, with no brain involved.
- **How it works:**
  - The network compares strain while “held” versus “released,” then rewires spring lengths when motor forces cross a threshold.
  - That update rule is temporal contrastive learning—the same compare-and-adjust logic used to train modern AI embeddings.
  - Learning still works when network parts turn over, and the same machinery can support mechanical adaptation and homeostasis.
- **Proof:**
  - [Learning via Mechanosensitivity and Activity in Cytoskeletal Networks | PRX Life](https://doi.org/10.1103/s7tg-6q4q)
  - [Learning via mechanosensitivity and activity in cytoskeletal networks - PMC](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12045384/)
- **Easy to miss because:** Learning is still framed as neurons and synapses—not sticky filaments that rewrite themselves from squeeze history alone.
- **Image:** https://arxiv.org/html/2504.15107v1/x1.png

### Insight 3: Speed alone evolves error correction
- **In short:** Life’s expensive “proofreading” steps may exist mainly because fixing a mistake is faster than letting the copy machine stall—not because accuracy was the goal.
- **How it works:**
  - When a wrong DNA letter makes the polymerase hang, the whole copy job slows; undoing the error can shorten total time even after paying an energy cost.
  - Simulations picking only for fast replication still evolve more proofreading when stall times are long or variable.
  - The same logic extends to multicomponent self-assembly, where “dynamic instability” can appear from speed pressure alone.
- **Proof:**
  - [Evolution of error correction through a need for speed | Science](https://www.science.org/doi/10.1126/science.adt1275)
  - [UChicago scientists clock a driving factor in the evolution of error correction | University of Chicago News](https://news.uchicago.edu/story/uchicago-scientists-clock-driving-factor-evolution-error-correction)
- **Easy to miss because:** Textbooks still teach proofreading as a fidelity tax—you pay time and ATP to avoid errors, full stop.
- **Image:** https://arxiv.org/html/2405.10911v3/x1.png

### Insight 4: Close planet makes its star flare
- **In short:** A young hot Jupiter orbiting every 6.95 days appears to trigger its star’s flares on schedule—and faces about six times more flare hits than it would on a quiet star.
- **How it works:**
  - Five years of TESS and CHEOPS light curves show 15 flares clustering near the inner planet’s transit phase, not random stellar noise.
  - The pattern fits a steady magnetic link: the planet perturbs field lines and flares fire where those lines meet the surface.
  - That extra radiation may explain why Webb sees an unusually puffed-up atmosphere on the same world.
- **Proof:**
  - [Close-in planet induces flares on its host star | Nature](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41586-025-09236-z)
  - [Discovery Alert: Flaring Star, Toasted Planet | NASA Science](https://science.nasa.gov/universe/exoplanets/discovery-alert-flaring-star-toasted-planet/)
- **Easy to miss because:** Exoplanet weather stories focus on the star scolding the planet—not the planet provoking the star on every lap.
- **Image:** https://media.springernature.com/full/springer-static/image/art%3A10.1038%2Fs41586-025-09236-z/MediaObjects/41586_2025_9236_Fig2_HTML.png

### Insight 5: Phage sponge theft triggers suicide
- **In short:** Some bacteria keep a toxic membrane weapon permanently caged with a steady supply of cyclic nucleotide “brakes”—and when a phage steals those molecules, the host kills itself to stop the infection.
- **How it works:**
  - The Panoptes operon pairs a tiny Cas10-like enzyme OptS with a membrane effector OptS; OptS constantly makes 2′,3′-c-di-AMP that keeps OptE inactive.
  - Phage anti-immunity protein Acb2 acts as a nucleotide sponge; clearing the brake lets OptE oligomerize and collapse the inner membrane.
  - Phages that lose Acb2 escape Panoptes—turning the phage’s own immune-evasion tool into the tripwire.
- **Proof:**
  - [The Panoptes system uses decoy cyclic nucleotides to defend against phage | Nature](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41586-025-09557-z)
  - [Turning a phage anti-defense weapon into an immunity trigger | PLOS Biology](https://journals.plos.org/plosbiology/article?id=10.1371/journal.pbio.3003978)
- **Easy to miss because:** Antiphage defense is still drawn as “detect virus → make alarm → kill”—not “guard a full pool and detonate when the thief arrives.”
- **Image:** https://media.springernature.com/full/springer-static/image/art%3A10.1038%2Fs41586-025-09557-z/MediaObjects/41586_2025_9557_Fig5_HTML.png

insights.title: Cell skeleton learns without neurons
insights.takeaway: A computer model of the actin–myosin cell skeleton can learn input–output force rules the same way contrastive AI does—using force-sensitive proteins and motors, with no brain involved.
insights.how:
- The network compares strain while “held” versus “released,” then rewires spring lengths when motor forces cross a threshold.

insights.title: Speed alone evolves error correction
insights.takeaway: Life’s expensive “proofreading” steps may exist mainly because fixing a mistake is faster than letting the copy machine stall—not because accuracy was the goal.
insights.how:
- When a wrong DNA letter makes the polymerase hang, the whole copy job slows; undoing the error can shorten total time even after paying an energy cost.
  - Simulations picking only for fast replication still evolve more proofreading when stall times are long or variable.
  - The same logic extends to multicomponent self-assembly, where “dynamic instability” can appear from speed pressure alone.
insights.proof:
- [Evolution of error correction through a need for speed | Science](https://www.science.org/doi/10.1126/science.adt1275)
  - [UChicago scientists clock a driving factor in the evolution of error correction | University of Chicago News](https://news.uchicago.edu/story/uchicago-scientists-clock-driving-factor-evolution-error-correction)
insights.miss: Textbooks still teach proofreading as a fidelity tax—you pay time and ATP to avoid errors, full stop.

insights.title: Close planet makes its star flare
insights.takeaway: A young hot Jupiter orbiting every 6.95 days appears to trigger its star’s flares on schedule—and faces about six times more flare hits than it would on a quiet star.
insights.how:
- Five years of TESS and CHEOPS light curves show 15 flares clustering near the inner planet’s transit phase, not random stellar noise.
  - The pattern fits a steady magnetic link: the planet perturbs field lines and flares fire where those lines meet the surface.
  - That extra radiation may explain why Webb sees an unusually puffed-up atmosphere on the same world.

insights.title: Phage sponge theft triggers suicide
insights.takeaway: Some bacteria keep a toxic membrane weapon permanently caged with a steady supply of cyclic nucleotide “brakes”—and when a phage steals those molecules, the host kills itself to stop the infection.
insights.how:
- The Panoptes operon pairs a tiny Cas10-like enzyme OptS with a membrane effector OptS; OptS constantly makes 2′,3′-c-di-AMP that keeps OptE inactive.
  - Phage anti-immunity protein Acb2 acts as a nucleotide sponge; clearing the brake lets OptE oligomerize and collapse the inner membrane.
  - Phages that lose Acb2 escape Panoptes—turning the phage’s own immune-evasion tool into the tripwire.
insights.proof:

  - [Turning a phage anti-defense weapon into an immunity trigger | PLOS Biology](https://journals.plos.org/plosbiology/article?id=10.1371/journal.pbio.3003978)
insights.miss: Antiphage defense is still drawn as “detect virus → make alarm → kill”—not “guard a full pool and detonate when the thief arrives.”

Searching for recent, verifiable developments not covered in the prior list, with two independent sources each.


### Insight 1: Water bridges carry heat before electricity
- **In short:** In a gold scanning-tunneling gap, heat can flow strongly while no electrical current can yet pass — because invisible water filaments bridge the gap.
- **How it works:**
  - A custom thermal microscope measured gold tips separated by a few nanometers and saw thermal conductance of a few nanowatts per kelvin before any measurable electron tunneling.
  - The team matched those curves with molecular dynamics where hydration layers on gold grow a capillary water meniscus between tip and sample.
  - That explains years of “mystery heat” in nanogaps without invoking exotic phonon tunneling or near-field radiation alone.
- **Proof:** Exactly 2 lines, each: `[Heat transfer in metallic nanometre-sized gaps | Nature Communications](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41467-025-62672-3)` — one line per independent source that agrees on the core claim.
  `[Heat transfer in metallic nanometre-sized gaps (PubMed)](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/40783387/)`
- **Easy to miss because:** Nanoscale heat stories usually assume vacuum gaps and quantum radiation — not ordinary adsorbed water in “high vacuum.”
- **Image:** none

### Insight 2: Two sky surveys see dark energy fade
- **In short:** The largest 3D galaxy map plus a separate all-sky survey both fit better if the force pushing the universe apart has been weakening — not staying constant forever.
- **How it works:**
  - DESI’s first three years mapped nearly 15 million galaxies and quasars and tracked how cosmic “standard rulers” stretched over 11 billion years.
  - Combined with microwave-background, supernova, and lensing data, the mismatch with a fixed dark-energy constant reached about 2.8 to 4.2 sigma.
  - The Dark Energy Survey’s final baryon-acoustic and supernova release independently reported a similar roughly 3.2 sigma pull toward evolving dark energy.
- **Proof:** Exactly 2 lines, each: `[New DESI Results Strengthen Hints That Dark Energy May Evolve – Berkeley Lab](https://newscenter.lbl.gov/2025/03/19/new-desi-results-strengthen-hints-that-dark-energy-may-evolve/)`
  `[Is Dark Energy Getting Weaker? New Evidence Strengthens the Case. | Quanta Magazine](https://www.quantamagazine.org/is-dark-energy-getting-weaker-new-evidence-strengthens-the-case-20250319/)`
- **Easy to miss because:** Headlines still treat dark energy as an unchanging cosmological constant baked into the standard model.
- **Image:** none

### Insight 3: Diamond flaws map megabar superconductors
- **In short:** Nitrogen-vacancy defects inside the diamond anvil itself can photograph the Meissner effect in a superhydride at megabar pressure — and reveal patchy superconductivity at the micron scale.
- **How it works:**
  - Researchers implanted a shallow NV layer in a specially cut diamond anvil and kept quantum magnetometry working above about 140 gigapascals.
  - In cerium hydride (CeH₉) they saw resistance drop near about 90 kelvin while local diamagnetism and trapped flux appeared in the same run.
  - Spatial maps showed superconducting regions were strongly inhomogeneous — not a uniform bulk switch — at sub-micron resolution where ordinary probes fail.
- **Proof:** Exactly 2 lines, each: `[Imaging the Meissner effect in hydride superconductors using quantum sensors | Nature](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41586-024-07026-7)`
  `[Imaging the Meissner effect and flux trapping in a hydride superconductor at megabar pressures (arXiv)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2306.03122)`
- **Easy to miss because:** Room-temperature superconductor hype focuses on resistance drops — not quantum cameras inside the press that sees where superconductivity actually lives.
- **Image:** none

### Insight 4: Linked superconductors fail like epidemics
- **In short:** Coupled superconducting wire networks can sit for thousands of seconds in a noisy middle state — then flip globally when random local “outbreaks” hit a branching factor of exactly one.
- **How it works:**
  - Interdependent superconducting segments thermally tug on neighbors, producing abrupt normal-to-super transitions unlike smooth textbook phase changes.
  - Before the flip, resistance plateaus for thousands of seconds while spontaneous cascades fire at random locations across the array.
  - The average branching factor equals one at critical bias, below one in the stable regime, and above one when collapse is imminent — like epidemic reproduction number R.
- **Proof:** Exactly 2 lines, each: `[The random cascading origin of abrupt transitions in interdependent systems | Nature Communications](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41467-025-61127-z)`
  `[The random cascading origin of abrupt transitions in interdependent systems (PubMed)](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/40593740/)`
- **Easy to miss because:** Phase transitions are taught as driven by one global control knob — not internal random cascades with early-warning statistics.
- **Image:** none

### Insight 5: Lab splits vacuum noise from light
- **In short:** Physicists finally measured vacuum fluctuations and light emitted by sources as separate, causal contributions — in a tabletop crystal with paired ultrafast pulses.
- **How it works:**
  - Two near-infrared pulses in zinc telluride mimic Fermi’s 1932 two-atom thought experiment using ultrafast optics instead of real atoms.
  - Vacuum fluctuations and source radiation correlated different light quadratures, so phase-sensitive detection could isolate each piece.
  - The split supports a quantum time-domain fluctuation–dissipation picture that textbooks argued could never be tested directly.
- **Proof:** Exactly 2 lines, each: `[Experimentally separating vacuum fluctuations from source radiation | Nature Communications](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41467-026-69142-4)`
  `[Experimentally separating vacuum fluctuations from source radiation (arXiv)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2502.18208)`
- **Easy to miss because:** Lamb shifts, Casimir forces, and spontaneous emission are still explained as if “empty vacuum” and “real emission” cannot be untangled experimentally.
- **Image:** none

Searching for recent, well-sourced developments that aren't on the exclusion list, with two independent confirmations per insight.
### Insight 1: Sideways eggs survive drops better
- **In short:** An egg needs the same peak force to crack either way—but on its side it squashes about 30% farther and survives low drops far more often.
- **How it works:**
  - MIT engineers tested more than 200 eggs and ran 180 controlled drops from 8–10 mm heights.
  - Both orientations broke at roughly 45 newtons, but horizontal eggs absorbed about 30% more energy before the shell failed.
  - Side-on shells act softer, so they soak up impact like bent knees instead of snapping like a stiff pole.
- **Proof:**
  - [Challenging common notions on how eggs break and the role of strength versus toughness](https://www.nature.com/articles/s42005-025-02087-0)
  - [Eggs less likely to crack when dropped side-on](https://phys.org/news/2025-05-eggs-side-reveals.html)
- **Easy to miss because:** The classic egg-drop lesson treats “stiffer end-first” as “stronger,” mixing up stiffness with toughness.
- **Image:** https://news.mit.edu/sites/default/files/images/202504/MIT-Dynamic-egg-Testing.jpg

### Insight 2: Nonlinear chips funnel any input
- **In short:** In a special lossless optical lattice, light shot in from almost any port still collapses into one bright spot—like heat draining to the coldest corner.
- **How it works:**
  - Researchers built nonlinear “time-synthetic” mesh lattices where photons interact with each other while total power stays conserved.
  - The lattice first spreads modes (a Joule–Thomson-like optical expansion), then thermalizes so almost all power sits in the lowest mode.
  - A 20-channel demo reported more than 70% port-to-port funneling efficiency—impossible if the chip behaved like ordinary linear optics.
- **Proof:**
  - [Universal routing of light via optical thermodynamics](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41566-025-01756-4)
  - [Conservative port-to-port funneling of light in nonlinear photonic lattices](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41467-025-64691-6)
- **Easy to miss because:** Conservative optics textbooks say you cannot merge unrelated inputs into one channel without absorbing or throwing away energy.
- **Image:** none

### Insight 3: Static mosaics turbocharge turbulent hits
- **In short:** Dust in turbulent air can clump up to ten thousand times tighter than fluid math predicts—because each collision paints patchy static charges that pull neighbors in harder.
- **How it works:**
  - Hollow glass spheres in a high-Reynolds turbulence chamber showed near-contact clustering about 10⁴ times above standard simulation forecasts.
  - Collisions leave uneven “mosaic” surface charge; those dipoles attract and trigger more collisions—a loop the team calls IMPACT.
  - Measured inward accelerations matched dipole–dipole predictions when rescaled by the measured charge maps over ten minutes.
- **Proof:**
  - [Amplification of particle collision through contact electrification in isotropic turbulence](https://www.pnas.org/doi/10.1073/pnas.2507580122)

insights.title: Nonlinear chips funnel any input

Searching for five fresh, cross-verified insights on topics not covered in your prior list.


### Insight 1: Astrocyte leaflets merge many synapses
- **In short:** Brain support cells can listen to many neurons at once through tiny “leaflet” pockets—not one synapse at a time.
- **How it works:**
  - Electron microscopy shows leaflets under 250 nm wide wrap about 90% of synapses in clusters, not alone.
  - Gap junctions link leaflets into one shared calcium domain with endoplasmic-reticulum pockets but no mitochondria.
  - Calcium spikes from different neurons merge inside a leaflet, using IP3R1—not the usual somatic IP3R2 channel.
- **Proof:** Exactly 2 lines, each: `[Astrocytes functionally integrate multiple synapses via specialized leaflet domains](https://www.cell.com/cell/fulltext/S0092-8674(25)01028-1)` — one line per independent source that agrees on the core claim.
  - `[Astrocytes, the unexpected conductors of brain networks](https://sciencesources.eurekalert.org/news-releases/1099196)`
- **Easy to miss because:** Textbooks still treat astrocytes as side helpers at single “tripartite” synapses, not multi-synapse integrators.
- **Image:** none

### Insight 2: Purine brake works without its chemistry
- **In short:** A famous “DNA-building-block” enzyme can shut purine factories down by holding another enzyme—without doing its own cutting job.
- **How it works:**
  - When cells recycle purines, NUDT5 binds PPAT, the rate-limiting step in de novo purine synthesis.
  - That contact forces PPAT into inactive oligomers and breaks apart purinosomes, the multi-enzyme purine factories.
  - Mutations that block binding—but leave catalysis intact—still let purines run wild and can resist thiopurine cancer drugs.
- **Proof:** Exactly 2 lines, each: `[NUDT5 regulates purine metabolism and thiopurine sensitivity by interacting with PPAT](https://www.science.org/doi/10.1126/science.adx9717)` — one line per independent source that agrees on the core claim.
  - `[A non-enzymatic role of Nudix hydrolase 5 in repressing purine de novo synthesis](https://doi.org/10.1126/science.adv4257)`
- **Easy to miss because:** NUDT5 was filed under “hydrolase that cleaves nucleotides,” not “scaffold that oligomerizes PPAT.”
- **Image:** https://cdn.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/blobs/194b/7618541/17c1db64288c/EMS210477-f001.jpg

### Insight 3: Immune enzyme tames radicals quantumly
- **In short:** Your antiviral enzyme viperin may leash dangerous radicals with quantum Coulomb forces—not just ordinary chemistry.
- **How it works:**
  - High-level simulations of viperin/RSAD2 track a metastable deprotonated ribose radical during CTP conversion.
  - Spin–charge exchange–correlation interactions—a quantum Coulomb effect—stabilize that intermediate by roughly 2–6 pKa units.
  - Because charged groups are everywhere in proteins, the team argues this may be a general radical-control trick in thousands of radical SAM enzymes.
- **Proof:** Exactly 2 lines, each: `[Quantum Coulombic Interactions Mediate Free Radical Control in Radical SAM Viperin/RSAD2](https://pubs.acs.org/doi/abs/10.1021/jacs.5c00572)` — one line per independent source that agrees on the core claim.
  - `[Quantum discovery reveals how enzymes tame free radicals](https://www.eurekalert.org/news-releases/1092095)`
- **Easy to miss because:** Radical enzymes are usually explained with iron–oxygen intermediates, not quantum electrostatic stabilization of the radical itself.
- **Image:** none

### Insight 4: RNA slips in mitochondrial DNA inflame
- **In short:** When RNA building blocks get stitched into mitochondrial DNA, the mistake can spill DNA into the cell and trigger inflammation—fixable with DNA sugar supplements.
- **How it works:**
  - Nucleotide imbalance lets ribonucleotides incorporate into mtDNA in aging mice, MGME1-deficient kidneys, and senescent cells.
  - Mitochondria lack the nuclear “RNA-letter removal” repair pathway, so the damage persists and mtDNA leaks into the cytosol.
  - That activates cGAS–STING signaling and the senescence secretory program; extra deoxyribonucleosides can suppress the cascade.
- **Proof:** Exactly 2 lines, each: `[Ribonucleotide incorporation into mitochondrial DNA drives inflammation](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41586-025-09541-7)` — one line per independent source that agrees on the core claim.
  - `[Ribonucleotide incorporation into mitochondrial DNA drives inflammation - PMC](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12629987/)`
- **Easy to miss because:** Inflammation stories focus on mtDNA “leaking out,” not on RNA-letter typos during replication as the upstream trigger.
- **Image:** https://cdn.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/blobs/1a61/12629987/1c4d8d0de563/41586_2025_9541_Fig1_HTML.jpg

### Insight 5: Robot maps chemistry hyperspaces fast
- **In short:** A cheap robot can scan thousands of reaction conditions by color alone—and prove yields usually change smoothly while still hiding sudden product swaps.
- **How it works:**
  - The platform runs roughly 1,000 reactions per day and reads product and by-product amounts mainly from UV–visible spectra.
  - Across more than 9,000 conditions, the team mathematically shows individual yields vary slowly when temperature or concentration change continuously.
  - Tight jumps in ingredient ratios still flip the main product and expose hidden networks—even in reactions known for over a century.
- **Proof:** Exactly 2 lines, each: `[Robot-assisted mapping of chemical reaction hyperspaces and networks](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41586-025-09490-1)` — one line per independent source that agrees on the core claim.
  - `[Robot-assisted mapping of chemical reaction hyperspaces and networks](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/40993255/)`
- **Easy to miss because:** Automation hype centers on AI guessing outcomes, not on a proof that chemistry landscapes are mostly smooth yet riddled with discrete switch points.
- **Image:** none

### Insight 1: Chip measures gravity with atoms
- **In short:** A ordinary silicon photonics chip can now run cold-atom gravity sensing that used to need a room-sized laser stack.
- **How it works:** Sandia built a chip modulator that shifts laser light for rubidium atom interferometry on an 8×8 mm die.
- Unwanted sidebands drop 47.8 decibels—roughly 100,000×—so stray light does not wreck the quantum fringes.
- With that chip in the loop, the team read gravity as about 9.77 ± 0.01 m/s² from atom-interferometer fringes.

### Insight 2: Ti:sapphire laser fits on chip
- **In short:** The lab workhorse titanium–sapphire laser can sit on a sliver of chip and start lasing from a cheap green diode, not a power-hungry pump laser.
- **How it works:** Stanford etched titanium–sapphire into nanoscale waveguides on a sapphire-on-insulator stack with whispering-gallery resonators.
- One demo device lased with only about 290 microwatts of pump power inside the resonator.
- The same platform amplified picosecond pulses to about 1 kilowatt peak power and ran a tunable laser array for a silicon-carbide quantum-optics test.
- **Proof:** Exactly 2 lines:
  - [Titanium:sapphire-on-insulator integrated lasers and amplifiers](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41586-024-07457-2)
  - [A chip-scale titanium-sapphire laser](https://engineering.stanford.edu/news/chip-scale-titanium-sapphire-laser)
- **Easy to miss because:** Ti:sapphire is still treated as a bulky, expensive room fixture—not something you could mass-print like other chip lasers.
- **Image:** https://www.nature.com/articles/s41586-024-07457-2/figures/1

### Insight 3: DNA knots hold meiosis zipper
- **In short:** During egg-and-sperm formation, branched DNA junctions do more than swap genes—they actively keep the chromosome “zipper” from falling apart too soon.
- **How it works:** In yeast, researchers could resolve Holliday junctions on command after chromosomes had already synapsed.
- Clearing those junctions made the synaptonemal complex—the meiotic zipper—disassemble, even though chromosome axis loops stayed intact.
- ZMM repair proteins and junctions feed back on each other: proteins protect junctions, and junctions keep proteins parked at future crossover sites until the cell is ready.
- **Proof:** Exactly 2 lines:
  - [Holliday junction–ZMM protein feedback enables meiotic crossover assurance](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41586-025-09559-x)
  - [Protecting double Holliday junctions ensures crossing over during meiosis](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41586-025-09555-1)
- **Easy to miss because:** Holliday junctions are usually taught as short-lived repair steps, not as structural switches that gate whole-chromosome pairing.
- **Image:** https://www.nature.com/articles/s41586-025-09559-x/figures/1

### Insight 4: Crocodile scales fold from squeeze
- **In short:** The polygonal “cracked mud” scales on a crocodile’s face are not tension cracks—they are wrinkles from skin growing faster than it can spread.
- **How it works:** A 2024 Nature study injected growth factor into Nile crocodile eggs and got wildly folded head skin and smaller scale tiles like a caiman’s.
- Light-sheet microscopy plus a 3D growth model matched normal and perturbed patterns when compressive folding—not tensile cracking—drove the shape.
- That overturns the famous 2012 story that jaw growth pulls keratinized skin apart like drying mud.
- **Proof:** Exactly 2 lines:
  - [Self-organized patterning of crocodile head scales by compressive folding](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41586-024-08268-1)
  - [Crocodile Head Scales Are Not Developmental Units But Emerge from Physical Cracking](https://www.science.org/doi/10.1126/science.1226265)
- **Easy to miss because:** Crocodile head scales remain the textbook poster child for “physics cracks the skin”—the stress direction was wrong.
- **Image:** https://www.nature.com/articles/s41586-024-08268-1/figures/2

### Insight 5: Protected qubits outlive their parts
- **In short:** Google’s Willow processor finally showed the textbook dream: stitch more physical qubits into a code, and the logical qubit lasts longer—not shorter.
- **How it works:** On a distance-7 surface code, logical error per cycle fell to about 0.143% as the lattice grew from 3×3 to 5×5 to 7×7 qubits.
- Each step up in code distance suppressed errors by a factor of about 2.14—exponential improvement, the signature of operating below threshold.
- The best logical memory lived about 2.4× longer than its strongest single physical qubit, crossing the “breakeven” line theorists have chased for decades.
- **Proof:** Exactly 2 lines:
  - [Quantum error correction below the surface code threshold](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41586-024-08449-y)
  - [Making quantum error correction work](https://research.google/blog/making-quantum-error-correction-work/)
- **Easy to miss because:** Headlines still focus on raw qubit counts, not the moment error-corrected information finally beats the hardware it is built from.
- **Image:** https://www.nature.com/articles/s41586-024-08449-y/figures/1

runs.markdown:
Searching for recent, verifiable discoveries that don't overlap the exclusion list.


### Insight 1: Tryptophan unlocks a ribosome hairpin trap
- **In short:** A 14-amino-acid chain in *E. coli* can fold into a tiny hairpin that blocks the ribosome at a stop codon — and tryptophan is the off switch.
- **How it works:**
  - Cryo-EM caught peptide PepNL folding back at the ribosome tunnel mouth, stalling translation at UGA.
  - Distorted isoleucine-13 physically blocks release factor RF2’s GGQ “scissors” from reaching the active site.
  - Extra tryptophan lets tryptophan-tRNA read through the stop codon — the opposite of peptides that need an inducer to stall.
- **Proof:**
  - [A mini-hairpin shaped nascent peptide blocks translation termination by a distinct mechanism | Nature Communications](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41467-025-57659-z)
  - [70S ribosome arrested by PepNL | EMDB EMD-60473](https://www.ebi.ac.uk/emdb/EMD-60473)
- **Easy to miss because:** Ribosome stalling is usually taught as “sense a small molecule, then freeze” — not “freeze by shape, release with an amino acid.”
- **Image:** none

### Insight 2: Rotavirus antibody trips one amino acid
- **In short:** A broadly neutralizing antibody can wreck rotavirus spikes by flipping a single phenylalanine — without blocking the binding site you’d expect.
- **How it works:**
  - Antibody 7H13 binds asymmetrically on the capsid-proximal side of spike protein VP4 across many genotypes.
  - Its heavy-chain isoleucine-54 shoves VP4 residue F418 out of a stabilizing pocket, unfolding the metastable spike.
  - Time-resolved cryo-EM and tomography show VP4 damage before adsorption — neutralization by destabilization, not classic receptor blockade.
- **Proof:**
  - [A single residue switch mediates the broad neutralization of Rotaviruses | Nature Communications](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41467-025-56114-3)
  - [Cryo-EM structure of simian rotavirus SA11 VP4 in complex with nAb 7H13 | RCSB PDB 8YGS](https://www.rcsb.org/structure/8YGS)
- **Easy to miss because:** Vaccine design still favors “mask the attachment knob” — this class of spike needs a internal switch broken.
- **Image:** none

### Insight 3: Recycling motor yanks bacteria open
- **In short:** Your cell’s p97/VCP “unfolder” can kill cytosolic bacteria by ripping tagged surface proteins out — like peeling a label until the bag bursts.
- **How it works:**
  - Intracellular bacteria get K48-polyubiquitinated; p97 with cofactors NPLOC4 and UFD1 latches on.
  - ATP-powered extraction pulls membrane proteins outward with enough force to tear the envelope.
  - Reconstitution in a test tube and mouse sepsis models show the same step is required — not proteasome grinding alone.
- **Proof:**
  - [Host AAA-ATPase VCP/p97 lyses ubiquitinated intracellular bacteria as an innate antimicrobial defence | Nature Microbiology](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41564-025-01984-y)
  - [Extract to lyse bacterial pathogens | Nature Microbiology](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41564-025-01995-9)
- **Easy to miss because:** Ubiquitin on pathogens is framed as “tag for the shredder” — here the tag triggers mechanical lysis first.
- **Image:** none

### Insight 4: Lead-208 stretches when excited
- **In short:** Lead-208 — the heaviest “doubly magic,” textbook-stable nucleus — still prefers rugby-ball shaping in its lowest excited vibrations.
- **How it works:**
  - Four Coulomb-excitation experiments measured large negative spectroscopic quadrupole moments for the 3₁⁻ and 2₁⁺ states.
  - Those moments imply time-averaged prolate (elongated) deformation even though magic numbers push toward a sphere.
  - Three major theory methods get the sign or size wrong — decades of precision data still miss this collectivity.
- **Proof:**
  - [Deformation and Collectivity in Doubly Magic ²⁰⁸Pb | Physical Review Letters](https://journals.aps.org/prl/abstract/10.1103/PhysRevLett.134.062502)
  - [Breakthrough study challenges long-held beliefs about the shape of atomic nuclei | University of Surrey](https://www.surrey.ac.uk/news/breakthrough-study-challenges-long-held-beliefs-about-shape-atomic-nuclei)
- **Easy to miss because:** “Doubly magic” is shorthand for “frozen round shell” — excitations can still carry strong quadrupole personality.
- **Image:** none

### Insight 5: Fab photonic qubits read ninety-nine percent
- **In short:** Quantum bits made from light can now be prepared and measured with 99.98% fidelity on chips built like ordinary silicon electronics — not one-off optical benches.
- **How it works:**
  - PsiQuantum’s Omega platform integrates sources, switches, and superconducting single-photon detectors in a GlobalFoundries 45 nm flow.
  - Benchmarked dual-rail qubits hit 99.98% ± 0.01% state preparation and measurement fidelity when a photon is detected.
  - Two-photon interference, two-qubit fusion, and chip-to-chip links all score near 99% in the same manufacturable stack (loss handled separately).
- **Proof:**
  - [A manufacturable platform for photonic quantum computing | Nature](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41586-025-08820-7)
  - [A quantum computing startup says it is already making millions of light-powered chips | Phys.org](https://phys.org/news/2025-03-quantum-startup-millions-powered-chips.html)
- **Easy to miss because:** Photonic quantum computing is still caricatured as fragile lab optics — this is wafer-scale integration with telecom-era fabrication.
- **Image:** none

### Insight 1: Pirate capsids steal foreign phage tails
- **In short:** Some bacterial parasites build virus heads with no tail, then snap on a neighbor phage’s tail to infect new species.
- **How it works:**
  - Capsid-forming phage-inducible chromosomal islands release tailless particles that carry their own DNA but cannot enter cells alone.
  - During a normal phage infection, leftover tails from other viruses float free and dock onto those head-only particles.
  - Whichever tail gets attached sets the target bacteria, so one island DNA package can ride into entirely different hosts.
- **Proof:**
  - [Chimeric infective particles expand species boundaries in phage-inducible chromosomal island mobilization](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.cell.2025.08.019)
  - [‘Microbial piracy’ uncovers new way to fight drug-resistant infections](https://www.imperial.ac.uk/news/articles/medicine/infectious-disease/2025/microbial-piracy-uncovers-new-way-to-fight-drug-resistant-infections/)
- **Easy to miss because:** Phage “satellites” were assumed to need their helper virus’s whole particle, not mix-and-match parts like Lego.
- **Image:** none

### Insight 2: Room-temperature diamond maser amplifies continuously
- **In short:** A tabletop diamond maser can now boost microwave signals continuously at room temperature, with gain up to about 30 decibels.
- **How it works:**
  - Nitrogen-vacancy spins in diamond sit in a high-quality microwave cavity and get pumped with a simple green laser diode.
  - The setup runs in continuous wave mode, not short pulses, which is what earlier room-temperature diamond masers could not do as amplifiers.
  - The same hardware can also act like a virtual cold load, pulling circuit noise down to an effective temperature near 66 kelvin without a fridge.
- **Proof:**
  - [Room-Temperature Solid-State Maser Amplifier](https://journals.aps.org/prx/abstract/10.1103/PhysRevX.14.041066)
  - [A Room-Temperature Solid-State Maser Amplifier](https://arxiv.org/html/2405.07486)
- **Easy to miss because:** Masers are taught as museum pieces that only work cryogenically, not as benchtop microwave amps.
- **Image:** none

### Insight 3: Split RNA gates run six-input logic
- **In short:** Engineered split-intron RNAs in bacteria can read up to six different inputs and still splice one output RNA correctly.
- **How it works:**
  - SENTR regulators use designed external guide sequences so RNA pieces rejoin only when trigger RNAs are present.
  - Many orthogonal versions can sit on one gene at once, wiring AND, OR, and NOT style logic in the cell.
  - They can output either a new messenger RNA or a noncoding RNA, and can pair with split-intein chemistry for protein outputs too.
- **Proof:**
  - [Programmable trans-splicing riboregulators for complex cellular logic computation](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41589-024-01781-4)
  - [Programmable trans-splicing riboregulators for complex cellular logic computation (Zenodo record)](https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.13743081)
- **Easy to miss because:** Synthetic biology hype focuses on DNA circuits, not post-transcriptional RNA splicing as the logic layer.
- **Image:** none

### Insight 4: Metal signal tracks lifetime not orbits
- **In short:** In cobalt monosilicide, a magnetic oscillation frequency matches the difference of two electron orbits yet stays strong above 50 kelvin.
- **How it works:**
  - Shubnikov–de Haas measurements show a combination frequency that would require electrons to travel against the magnetic push for half a loop.
  - Ordinary Fermi-surface orbit signals fade within a few kelvin, but this difference signal survives beyond 50 kelvin.
  - Models fit if the wave is oscillating quasiparticle lifetime from inter-orbit scattering, not a new pocket of the Fermi surface.
- **Proof:**
  - [Quantum oscillations of the quasiparticle lifetime in a metal](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41586-023-06330-y)
  - [A Field Guide to Non‐Onsager Quantum Oscillations in Metals](https://doi.org/10.1002/apxr.202400134)
- **Easy to miss because:** Every new quantum oscillation peak is reflexively mapped to a hidden Fermi-surface sheet.
- **Image:** none

### Insight 5: Latch leg stores jump energy parallel
- **In short:** A 450-gram robot leg can latch springs in parallel, release them for big jumps, then return to fine stepping control.
- **How it works:**
  - Pinto uses twisted-string actuators and carbon-fiber springs inside a latched five-bar leg mechanism.
  - A latch lets elastic energy sit in parallel with the motor, storing more jump energy than series-elastic or motor-only legs at this scale.
  - Spined arms on sprung hinges grab bark after flight so the bot can perch on a vertical trunk like a squirrel tree jump.
- **Proof:**
  - [Pinto: A Latched Spring Actuated Robot for Jumping and Perching](https://doi.org/10.1109/ICRA55743.2025.11128584)
  - [Pinto: A latched spring actuated robot for jumping and perching](https://arxiv.org/html/2409.09203v1)
- **Easy to miss because:** Small legged robots are judged on steady walking, not mode-switching elasticity borrowed from arboreal mammals.
- **Image:** none

Searching for five fresh, cross-verified technical insights that don't overlap the prior list.


### Insight 1: Muscle RNA buds out of nucleus
- **In short:** When muscle cells switch on genes for giant proteins like titin, those oversized RNA messages leave the nucleus in membrane buds—not through the usual pore.
- **How it works:** Nuclear pores stretch to roughly 60 nanometers, but sarcomere RNAs can be far longer than that limit.
- During myotube formation, buds pinch from the inner nuclear membrane, carry internal vesicles, and load up those long muscle transcripts.
- A protein called UIF targets the RNA into buds, and ESCRT-III membrane scissors finish export—same machinery viruses hijack, now shown for your own genes.
- **Proof:** [Nuclear envelope budding enables export of large transcripts in muscle cells](https://www.cell.com/cell/fulltext/S0092-8674%2826%2900386-7)
- [Nuclear envelope budding is a non-canonical mechanism to export large transcripts in muscle cells](https://www.biorxiv.org/content/10.1101/2025.04.18.649598v2)
- **Easy to miss because:** Textbooks still treat the nuclear pore as the only door RNA uses to reach the cytoplasm.
- **Image:** none

### Insight 2: Squeeze turns archaea into tissue
- **In short:** Press a single salt-loving archaeon under an agar pad and it can stop dividing yet grow into a layered tissue—with central “scutoid” cells—without using its tubulin-like division protein FtsZ.
- **How it works:** Under compression above about 100 kilopascals, *Haloferax volcanii* cells enlarge into a multinucleate “soufflé” instead of splitting in two.
- After roughly 12 hours, membrane tension hits a threshold and the mass cellularizes through many septations at once, not classic binary fission.
- The result mimics animal epithelia: flat peripheral cells, tall central scutoids, and actin homolog volactin cables that stiffen the structure.
- **Proof:** [Tissue-like multicellular development triggered by mechanical compression in archaea](https://www.science.org/doi/10.1126/science.adu0047)
- [Growing together under pressure](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41579-025-01184-9)
- **Easy to miss because:** Multicellularity is usually framed as a rare eukaryote invention, not something a squeeze can wake in archaea.
- **Image:** none

### Insight 3: Cell teams feel stiffness one hundred micrometers deep
- **In short:** A sheet of epithelial cells can “feel” how stiff a buried layer is through more than 100 micrometers of collagen—about ten times farther than a lone migrating cell manages.
- **How it works:** In double-layer gels, collectives tug on collagen fibers and temporarily stiffen them, sending mechanical news downward.
- Stiffer bases slow early migration, keep clusters tighter, and only later let cells spread—behavior a model ties to how far the matrix deforms.
- Break collective force with myosin-II blockers or weakened cell–cell links, and the long-range stiffness sense vanishes.
- **Proof:** [Emergent depth-mechanosensing of epithelial collectives regulates cell clustering and dispersal on layered matrices](https://www.pnas.org/doi/10.1073/pnas.2423875122)
- [Working together, cells extend their senses](https://engineering.washu.edu/news/2025/Working-together-cells-extend-their-senses.html)
- **Easy to miss because:** Mechanosensing is taught as a contact sport at the cell’s feet, not a team sport that probes hidden tissue layers.
- **Image:** none

### Insight 4: AR glasses shed their projection lens
- **In short:** Stanford’s holographic AR stack mounts the light modulator almost flush to the waveguide—dropping the thick projection lens ordinary AR goggles need—while still painting full-color 3D scenes.
- **How it works:** Inverse-designed metasurface gratings (period about 384 nanometers) steer red, green, and blue into a dispersion-compensating waveguide.
- A phase-only modulator sits near the in-coupler, so the engine is no longer as thick as a lens focal length.
- A hybrid model mixes real wave physics with AI pieces trained from camera feedback, so holograms survive manufacturing quirks in a glasses-sized prototype.
- **Proof:** [Full-colour 3D holographic augmented-reality displays with metasurface waveguides](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41586-024-07386-0)
- [Holographic AR Glasses with Metasurface Waveguides | Nature 2024](https://www.computationalimaging.org/publications/holographicar/)
- **Easy to miss because:** AR hype focuses on bigger fields of view, not on deleting an entire optical chunk from the frame.
- **Image:** none

### Insight 5: Diffusion invents grippers without sensors
- **In short:** Stanford’s DGDM framework can dream up new robot finger shapes in about 0.8 seconds that rotate or shift objects using only a blind parallel squeeze—no cameras, no touch, no task-specific training run.
- **How it works:** A diffusion model proposes gripper geometry while a shared dynamics network scores how shapes will push objects.
- Gradients from that dynamics net guide diffusion like a classifier, steering designs toward a requested motion profile.
- On shift, rotate, and pose-align tasks, the generated hands beat optimization and unguided diffusion baselines by about 31.5% and 45.3% relative success.
- **Proof:** [Dynamics-Guided Diffusion Model for Sensor-less Robot Manipulator Design](https://proceedings.mlr.press/v270/xu25d.html)
- [How Machine Learning Brings Unconventional Robots to Life](http://ai.stanford.edu/blog/robopanoptes/)
- **Easy to miss because:** Robot design still assumes you add sensing and retrain per task—not that morphology alone can do the steering.
- **Image:** none

Searching for five fresh, cross-verified emerging-tech insights not covered in your prior list.


### Insight 1: Graphene heat and charge run opposite
- **In short:** In ultraclean graphene at the Dirac point, better electrical conduction can come with worse heat conduction—the opposite of ordinary metals.
- **How it works:**
  - IISc and NIMS teams measured both conductivities together and saw the Lorentz number break the Wiedemann–Franz rule by more than 200× at low temperature.
  - Near the Dirac point, electrons move as a collective “Dirac fluid,” so charge and heat follow different hydrodynamic channels.
  - Electrical conductivity still settles near about (4±1)×e²/h—a universal value tied to the quantum of conductance, not device details.
- **Proof:**
  - [Universality in quantum critical flow of charge and heat in ultraclean graphene](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41567-025-02972-z)
  - [Graphene shows how electrons can act like a perfect fluid](https://www.nature.com/articles/d44151-025-00170-7)
- **Easy to miss because:** Graphene headlines still treat it mainly as a fast wire, not a tabletop stand-in for quark–gluon plasma physics.
- **Image:** https://media.springernature.com/lw685/springer-static/image/art%3A10.1038%2Fs41567-025-02972-z/MediaObjects/41567_2025_2972_Fig2_HTML.png

### Insight 2: Brain mesh rides embryo folding
- **In short:** A sub-micrometer mesh laid on a flat embryonic neural plate can stretch and spread through the whole 3D brain as the embryo folds itself.
- **How it works:**
  - Harvard-led teams placed tissue-soft mesh electrodes on the neural plate before neurulation in frog and axolotl embryos.
  - As the plate rolls into a neural tube and then a full brain, the mesh deforms with the tissue instead of tearing or slipping out.
  - The same implants recorded single-neuron spikes for days—and in axolotls, electrical stimulation could speed regeneration after tail amputation.
- **Proof:**
  - [Brain implantation of soft bioelectronics via embryonic development](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41586-025-09106-8)
  - [Brain implantation of tissue-level-soft bioelectronics via embryonic development (PMC)](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12975305/)
- **Easy to miss because:** Brain-interface stories still assume adult surgery and stiff probes, not piggybacking on embryonic origami.
- **Image:** https://media.springernature.com/lw685/springer-static/image/art%3A10.1038%2Fs41586-025-09106-8/MediaObjects/41586_2025_9106_Fig1_HTML.png

### Insight 3: Split enzyme wraps RNA in ubiquitin
- **In short:** An immune protein named ZNFX1 completes its ubiquitin-ligase job only when two copies meet on viral RNA—and then glues RNA into dense, ubiquitin-coated clumps.
- **How it works:**
  - Cell and Molecular Cell teams showed ZNFX1’s E3 active site is split across the protein and only works when dimers form on single-stranded RNA tracks.
  - The enzyme tags both itself and the RNA, pulling strands into nucleoprotein particles that quarantine genetic material.
  - Patient mutations that break this pathway fail to trap RNA—and viruses replicate more freely.
- **Proof:**
  - [A split-site E3 ligase mechanism enables ZNFX1 to ubiquitinate and cluster single-stranded RNA into ubiquitin-coated nucleoprotein particles](https://www.cell.com/cell/fulltext/S0092-8674(25)00920-1)
  - [ZNFX1 uses two-component ubiquitin circuitry to quarantine viral RNA](https://www.cell.com/molecular-cell/fulltext/S1097-2765(26)00129-2)
- **Easy to miss because:** Antiviral immunity is still narrated as “detect and destroy,” not “tag RNA and physically cage it.”
- **Image:** https://ars.els-cdn.com/content/image/1-s2.0-S0092867425009201-gr3.jpg

### Insight 4: Reaction AI tracks every electron
- **In short:** MIT’s FlowER model predicts reaction mechanisms by moving electrons stepwise—and cannot invent or lose atoms because the math forbids it.
- **How it works:**
  - Published in Nature, FlowER represents molecules as bond–electron matrices and uses flow matching to morph reactants into products.
  - Every step must conserve mass and electrons, eliminating the “hallucinated atom” failures common in sequence-based reaction models.
  - It can rebuild full arrow-pushing pathways on new scaffolds and fine-tune to unseen reaction classes from only dozens of examples.
- **Proof:**
  - [Electron flow matching for generative reaction mechanism prediction](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41586-025-09426-9)
  - [A new generative AI approach to predicting chemical reactions (MIT News)](https://news.mit.edu/2025/generative-ai-approach-to-predicting-chemical-reactions-0903)
- **Easy to miss because:** Chemistry AI is usually sold on accuracy leaderboards, not on obeying Lavoisier-level conservation by design.
- **Image:** https://media.springernature.com/lw685/springer-static/image/art%3A10.1038%2Fs41586-025-09426-9/MediaObjects/41586_2025_9426_Fig1_HTML.png

### Insight 5: Chip neurons match real spike energy
- **In short:** Artificial neurons built from a bio-derived memristor can fire at roughly 70–130 millivolts and down to about 0.2 picojoules per spike—inside the biological range.
- **How it works:**
  - A Nature Communications team paired a protein-based memristor with a simple RC circuit to mimic integrate-and-fire behavior.
  - Spike amplitude, timing, frequency response, and energy were tuned to sit near published values for real neurons—not the volt-scale spikes typical of earlier chips.
  - Wired to a living cell, the device processed cellular signals in real time and responded to extracellular ions like a neuromodulated neuron.
- **Proof:**
  - [Constructing artificial neurons with functional parameters comprehensively matching biological values](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41467-025-63640-7)
  - [Constructing artificial neurons with functional parameters comprehensively matching biological values (NSF PAR)](https://par.nsf.gov/biblio/10649075-constructing-artificial-neurons-functional-parameters-comprehensively-matching-biological-values)
- **Easy to miss because:** Neuromorphic hardware demos still highlight “brain-like logic,” not matching the actual voltage and energy budget of a single spike.
- **Image:** https://media.springernature.com/lw685/springer-static/image/art%3A10.1038%2Fs41467-025-63640-7/MediaObjects/41467_2025_63640_Fig1_HTML.png

runs.markdown:
Searching for five fresh, cross-verified technical insights that don't overlap the exclusion list.


### Insight 1: Lysosomes brew cyanide from glycine
- **In short:** Your cells can make hydrogen cyanide inside acidic lysosomes from glycine—and at the right dose it acts like nitric oxide or hydrogen sulfide, not just poison.
- **How it works:**
  - Human cells and mouse blood carry measurable cyanide, and only glycine—not the other 19 amino acids—ramps production up.
  - Lysosomal peroxidases such as myeloperoxidase turn bleach-like HOCl and glycine into cyanide best around pH 4.5.
  - Too little or too much hurts mitochondria; in the sweet spot cyanide tags cysteines with S-cyanylation and can protect cells in hypoxia.
- **Proof:**
  - [Regulation of mammalian cellular metabolism by endogenous cyanide production](https://www.nature.com/articles/s42255-025-01225-w)
  - [Cyanide plays a major role in the human body, study reveals](https://medicalxpress.com/news/2025-03-cyanide-plays-major-role-human.html)
- **Easy to miss because:** Textbooks still treat cyanide as an external toxin, not a gas your own organelles manufacture on purpose.
- **Image:** none

### Insight 2: HIV hijacks a spliceosome helicase
- **In short:** HIV does not just land near active genes—it recruits the splicing helicase Aquarius to unwind DNA–RNA hybrids, then stitches its DNA into those spots.
- **How it works:**
  - In human CD4⁺ T cells, HIV integration hotspots line up with genomic R-loops—three-stranded DNA–RNA tangles—in gene introns.
  - Viral integrase binds those hybrids, but integration still needs Aquarius (AQR) from the intron-binding complex to resolve them.
  - Knocking out AQR cuts integration efficiency and pushes surviving insertions into quiet, R-loop-poor intergenic DNA.
- **Proof:**
  - [Aquarius helicase facilitates HIV-1 integration into R-loop enriched genomic regions](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41564-025-02089-2)
  - [Human immunodeficiency virus-1 induces host genomic R-loops and preferentially integrates its genome near the R-loop regions](https://elifesciences.org/articles/97348)
- **Easy to miss because:** Latency research still centers on chromatin openness, not on a spliceosome motor the virus borrows to open hybrid-DNA landing pads.
- **Image:** none

### Insight 3: Surface markers AND-gate new proteins
- **In short:** Engineers built living cells that stitch a full active protein together only when two chosen surface markers sit on the same cell—like a molecular AND gate with no computer.
- **How it works:**
  - The SMART platform splits a protein and an intein splicing module across two binders aimed at different antigens.
  - When both fragments meet on one membrane, trans-splicing fuses them into one working protein on that cell alone.
  - Teams showed AND, OR, and NOT logic, plus a version that releases interleukin-1β only from dual-marker cells in a mixed culture.
- **Proof:**
  - [Programmable protein ligation on cell surfaces](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41586-025-09287-2)
  - [SMART Protein Splicing Enables Programmable Cell Surfaces](https://www.bnl.gov/newsroom/news.php?a=222674)
- **Easy to miss because:** Immunotherapy still chases single biomarkers, even though one receptor rarely defines a diseased cell type.
- **Image:** none

### Insight 4: Fiber spots twins fifty times closer
- **In short:** A plain double-clad fiber can tell whether you are looking at one star or two even when they sit 50× closer than the usual diffraction limit—without building a sharper telescope first.
- **How it works:**
  - Light from the sky enters the fiber coupler and splits into core light versus higher-order modes.
  - The team compares multimode power to single-mode power to test “one source or two?” instead of trying to resolve two sharp dots.
  - For brightness differences under 5 dB, the setup still catches a hidden companion at separations 50× below the Rayleigh limit.
- **Proof:**
  - [Super-resolving binary-source hypothesis testing with a double-clad fiber coupler](https://doi.org/10.1364/ol.573054)
  - [On-sky Binary Source hypothesis testing beyond the diffraction limit using spatial mode demultiplexing based detection](https://arxiv.org/html/2606.18025)
- **Easy to miss because:** “Beat the diffraction limit” headlines assume bigger mirrors or exotic quantum cameras, not a mode-sorting fiber and a ratio meter.
- **Image:** none

### Insight 5: Current alone entangles photons on-chip
- **In short:** Injecting electric current into a hybrid chip now yields polarization-entangled photon pairs at about 4.5×10¹⁰ pairs per second per milliwatt—with no bulky external laser and no post-selection cleanup.
- **How it works:**
  - A distributed-feedback laser die is bonded to a thin-film lithium niobate photonic circuit with twin nonlinear waveguides, a splitter, and a polarization combiner.
  - Spontaneous down-conversion in the poled waveguides interferes on-chip to emit Bell states across a 73-nanometer bandwidth.
  - Bell-state fidelity stays above 96% across frequency channels—bright enough for wavelength-multiplexed quantum key distribution from a postage-stamp module.
- **Proof:**
  - [Electrically Pumped Ultrabright Entangled Photons on Chip](https://doi.org/10.1103/sfj2-dcx1)
  - [An electrically powered source of entangled light on a chip](https://phys.org/news/2026-01-electrically-powered-source-entangled-chip.html)
- **Easy to miss because:** Integrated quantum photonics still assumed a lab laser tethered to the chip; this treats entanglement like any other electrically pumped diode product.
- **Image:** none

insights.title: Fiber spots twins fifty times closer

- Light from the sky enters the fiber coupler and splits into core light versus higher-order modes.

  - For brightness differences under 5 dB, the setup still catches a hidden companion at separations 50× below the Rayleigh limit.

insights.title: Current alone entangles photons on-chip
insights.takeaway: Injecting electric current into a hybrid chip now yields polarization-entangled photon pairs at about 4.5×10¹⁰ pairs per second per milliwatt—with no bulky external laser and no post-selection cleanup.
insights.how:
- A distributed-feedback laser die is bonded to a thin-film lithium niobate photonic circuit with twin nonlinear waveguides, a splitter, and a polarization combiner.
  - Spontaneous down-conversion in the poled waveguides interferes on-chip to emit Bell states across a 73-nanometer bandwidth.
  - Bell-state fidelity stays above 96% across frequency channels—bright enough for wavelength-multiplexed quantum key distribution from a postage-stamp module.

runs.markdown:
Searching for recent, verifiable developments that don't overlap with the excluded list.


### Insight 1: Polymyxin kills only hungry bacteria
- **In short:** A last-resort antibiotic can bind starving bacteria yet fail to kill them — because the lethal step needs the cell to be actively making and shipping its outer armor.
- **How it works:** At clinical doses, polymyxin B wiped out growing *E. coli* but barely touched stationary-phase cells unless researchers fed them a carbon source.
- While the bug is metabolically active, ATP-driven lipopolysaccharide synthesis and transport strip large amounts of outer-membrane armor and create surface bulges seen by atomic force microscopy.
- That opened a path to the inner membrane, which the drug punctures without needing energy — and that final leak is what actually kills the cell.
- **Proof:** [Polymyxin B lethality requires energy-dependent outer membrane disruption](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41564-025-02133-1)
- [Polymyxin B lethality requires energy-dependent outer membrane disruption (bioRxiv)](https://doi.org/10.1101/2025.04.16.649083)
- **Easy to miss because:** Membrane-targeting drugs are usually sold as brute-force pore punchers, not as processes that hitch a ride on the bacterium’s own fuel cycle.
- **Image:** https://media.springernature.com/full/springer-static/image/art%3A10.1038%2Fs41564-025-02133-1/MediaObjects/41564_2025_2133_Fig6_HTML.jpg

### Insight 2: Mitotic loops overlap six megabases
- **In short:** Dividing cells may fold chromosomes with giant DNA loops that stack on top of one another — each loop spanning millions of DNA letters, not neat non-overlapping rungs.
- **How it works:** Nanoscale 3D DNA tracing in single mitotic cells found a sharp “closest approach” distance that bottoms out at about 6–8 megabases.
- Computer models fit only if condensin motors keep extruding loops at roughly 4 ± 2 kilobases per second and can pass through loops already in place.
- Those overlapping megabase loops pack DNA until chromatin’s own repulsion sets the limit — and that alone builds rod-shaped chromosomes without a separate rigid scaffold.
- **Proof:** [Nanoscale DNA tracing reveals the self-organization mechanism of mitotic chromosomes](https://www.cell.com/cell/fulltext/S0092-8674(25)00255-7)
- [Nanoscale DNA tracing reveals the self-organization mechanism of mitotic chromosomes (PMC)](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12127698/)
- **Easy to miss because:** Textbook mitosis art still favors tidy consecutive loops or helical staircases, not a messy pile of loops sharing the same DNA highway.
- **Image:** https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/instance/12127698/bin/nihms-2067674-f0001.jpg

### Insight 3: Stop DNA looping, grow lobed nuclei
- **In short:** You can turn a round immune-cell nucleus into a multi-lobed “flower petal” shape by shutting off the motor that normally loops DNA — and that shape flip alone switches on an infection-fighting gene program.
- **How it works:** In young neutrophil progenitors, removing the loop-extrusion loader NIPBL within hours produced horseshoe, banded, ringed, and hyper-segmented nuclei like mature neutrophils.
- Chromosomes lost ordinary topologically associating domain contacts and instead formed mega-loops and hubs wired to neutrophil-specific enhancers.
- Thousands of inflammatory genes turned on even though the cells had not finished normal differentiation — linking nuclear geometry directly to immune identity.
- **Proof:** [Nuclear morphology is shaped by loop-extrusion programs](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41586-024-07086-9)
- [Researchers uncover mechanisms behind enigmatic shapes of nuclei](https://www.eurekalert.org/news-releases/1034335)
- **Easy to miss because:** The famous segmented neutrophil nucleus is usually treated as a quirky anatomical badge, not as an output you can dial with genome-folding machinery.
- **Image:** https://media.springernature.com/full/springer-static/image/art%3A10.1038%2Fs41586-024-07086-9/MediaObjects/41586_2024_7086_Fig1_HTML.jpg

### Insight 4: Robot fingers sense slip via DC
- **In short:** Robot gripper skin can detect an object starting to slip by generating steady direct current when metal slides on conductive fabric — not by the familiar static-electricity spikes from rubbing.
- **How it works:** Titanium sliding on PEDOT:PSS-coated stretchable textile creates a tribovoltaic Schottky junction that outputs DC whose timing tracks slip speed.
- The team reports roughly three to four orders of magnitude higher current density than typical alternating-current triboelectric touch patches.
- Wired into robot fingers alongside a normal pressure sensor, the textile ran through about one million cycles and fed standard control code for grasp adjustment without extra power for the slip channel.
- **Proof:** [Slip-actuated bionic tactile sensing system with dynamic DC generator integrated E-textile for dexterous robotic manipulation](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41467-025-61843-6)
- [Slip-actuated bionic tactile sensing system with dynamic DC generator integrated E-textile for dexterous robotic manipulation (PubMed)](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/40739032/)
- **Easy to miss because:** Self-powered robot touch is dominated by triboelectric “zap when you rub” stories, not semiconductor junctions that behave like tiny sliding solar cells.
- **Image:** https://media.springernature.com/full/springer-static/image/art%3A10.1038%2Fs41467-025-61843-6/MediaObjects/41467_2025_Art_61843_Fig1_HTML.jpg

### Insight 5: Calcium turns fungal drug to Velcro
- **In short:** A mushroom-derived antibiotic does not just dock one-to-one on its bacterial target — calcium helps it oligomerize into a dense Velcro-like mat that traps the cell-wall building block lipid II.
- **How it works:** On bacterial membranes rich in lipid II, plectasin molecules snap together into supramolecular patches seen by atomic force microscopy and solid-state NMR.
- Calcium binds an acidic patch on the peptide (residues DEDD), stiffens a loop far from the binding site, and allosterically tightens grip on lipid II’s pyrophosphate headgroup.
- Even if one lipid II molecule escapes a single peptide, it remains inside the larger structure — so the bacterium cannot reuse that precursor to rebuild its wall.
- **Proof:** [Host defence peptide plectasin targets bacterial cell wall precursor lipid II by a calcium-sensitive supramolecular mechanism](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41564-024-01696-9)
- [Antibiotic ‘Velcro’ gives bacteria a sticky situation](https://www.uu.nl/en/news/antibiotic-velcro-gives-bacteria-a-sticky-situation-0)
- **Easy to miss because:** Antibiotic discovery still trains chemists to hunt for tighter single-molecule locks, not for drugs that only work after they crowd-source into a sticky net.
- **Image:** https://media.springernature.com/full/springer-static/image/art%3A10.1038%2Fs41564-024-01696-9/MediaObjects/41564_2024_1696_Fig1_HTML.jpg

runs.markdown:
Searching for recent, well-sourced developments that don't overlap the exclusion list.
### Insight 1: Heat builds cells without membranes
- **In short:** A warm–cool gap in a tiny water pore can pile up real cell machinery and switch on gene expression—no lipid bubble required.
- **How it works:**
  - In a 170-micrometer chamber, a dilute protein-synthesis mix was too weak to work until a temperature difference was applied.
  - Warm–cool flow plus thermophoresis (molecules drifting along the gradient) trapped components at the bottom and boosted green protein signal up to about 25-fold there.
  - With amino acids flowing in from above, models suggest roughly 80% of product can stay trapped for months instead of washing away.
- **Proof:**
  - [Membraneless protocell confined by a heat flow](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41567-025-02935-4)
  - [Membrane or metabolism, which came first?](https://www.eurekalert.org/news-releases/1088606)
- **Easy to miss because:** Origin-of-life stories still assume a fatty membrane had to show up before metabolism could start.
- **Image:** https://media.springernature.com/full/springer-static/image/art%3A10.1038%2Fs41567-025-02935-4/Fig1_HTML.png

### Insight 2: Optical AI reads digits photon-thin
- **In short:** A light-based neural network can recognize handwritten digits at 98% accuracy while using about 0.038 photons per multiply-add—far below the usual “need bright light” rule.
- **How it works:**
  - Researchers built a single-photon-detection optical network: the hidden layer “fires” on individual photon hits, not smooth bright signals.
  - Training explicitly treated each activation as a random draw from physics, not as tiny noise to ignore.
  - On MNIST digits, the full pipeline reached about 98.0% ± 1.3% test accuracy at roughly 0.038 detected photons per MAC at 532 nm.
- **Proof:**
  - [Quantum-limited stochastic optical neural networks operating at a few quanta per activation](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41467-024-55220-y)
  - [Quantum-limited stochastic optical neural networks operating at a few quanta per activation (PMC)](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11698857/)
- **Easy to miss because:** Analog and optical AI are still sold on turning up power until signal-to-noise is comfortably above ten.
- **Image:** https://media.springernature.com/full/springer-static/image/art%3A10.1038%2Fs41467-024-55220-y/Fig1_HTML.png

### Insight 3: One sugar reboots a stranded enzyme
- **In short:** Cells can keep a sugar-building enzyme alive by shipping in a fake intermediate made by a neighbor enzyme—not by flooding the compartment with fresh NAD⁺.
- **How it works:**
  - UXS1, which makes UDP-xylose for bone-related sugars, can stall with NADH stuck in its pocket when NAD⁺ is scarce in the endoplasmic reticulum.
  - TGDS makes UDP-4-keto-6-deoxyglucose, which mimics UXS1’s intermediate and finishes the stuck catalytic cycle inside the pocket.
  - Without that “enzyme-rescue metabolite,” UXS1 fails and a rare skeletal disorder called Catel–Manzke syndrome follows.

### Insight 4: Chaperone slack grows giant yeast clumps
- **In short:** Lab-evolved “snowflake” yeast can become more than 20,000 times bigger mainly by dialing down a folding helper—not by inventing a new structural gene.
- **How it works:**
  - In the Multicellularity Long-Term Evolution Experiment, larger, tougher yeast clusters converged on lower Hsp90 chaperone levels.
  - Less Hsp90 destabilizes the cell-cycle kinase Cdc28, delaying mitosis and stretching cells into long branches that tangle neighbors together.
  - Turning Hsp90 or Cdc28 back up shortened cells and shrank groups, cutting multicellular fitness under size selection.
- **Proof:**
  - [Proteostatic tuning underpins the evolution of novel multicellular traits](https://www.science.org/doi/10.1126/sciadv.adn2706)
  - [New study discovers how altered protein folding drives multicellular evolution](https://phys.org/news/2024-03-protein-multicellular-evolution.html)
- **Easy to miss because:** Evolution coverage still assumes new body plans need new DNA sequences, not retuned protein folding.
- **Image:** none

### Insight 5: Bone sensors plug into nerve chemistry
- **In short:** The hidden cells that sense bone strain sit next to cholinergic nerve fibers and use nicotinic receptors—like muscle—to tune how strongly bone responds to load.
- **How it works:**
  - Fluorescent imaging in live cortical bone showed osteocytes nestled against cholinergic nerve fibers in vivo.
  - Osteocyte-specific loss of receptor parts Chrna1 or Rapsn changed calcium responses to mechanical strain in sex-specific ways.
  - In females, small strains mattered less until exercise-like loading; in males, some groups became hypersensitive while bulk loading barely moved architecture.
- **Proof:**
  - [Cholinergic regulation of osteocyte mechanobiology: A paradigm for bone adaptation](https://doi.org/10.1126/sciadv.ads9720)
  - [A cholinergic neuroskeletal interface promotes bone formation during postnatal growth and exercise](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.stem.2022.02.008)
- **Easy to miss because:** Bone is still framed as a slow mechanical material, not a tissue wired into the autonomic nervous system.
- **Image:** none

insights.title: Heat builds cells without membranes
insights.takeaway: A warm–cool gap in a tiny water pore can pile up real cell machinery and switch on gene expression—no lipid bubble required.
insights.how:
- In a 170-micrometer chamber, a dilute protein-synthesis mix was too weak to work until a temperature difference was applied.
  - Warm–cool flow plus thermophoresis (molecules drifting along the gradient) trapped components at the bottom and boosted green protein signal up to about 25-fold there.
  - With amino acids flowing in from above, models suggest roughly 80% of product can stay trapped for months instead of washing away.

insights.title: Optical AI reads digits photon-thin
insights.takeaway: A light-based neural network can recognize handwritten digits at 98% accuracy while using about 0.038 photons per multiply-add—far below the usual “need bright light” rule.
insights.how:
- Researchers built a single-photon-detection optical network: the hidden layer “fires” on individual photon hits, not smooth bright signals.
  - Training explicitly treated each activation as a random draw from physics, not as tiny noise to ignore.
  - On MNIST digits, the full pipeline reached about 98.0% ± 1.3% test accuracy at roughly 0.038 detected photons per MAC at 532 nm.
insights.proof:
- [Quantum-limited stochastic optical neural networks operating at a few quanta per activation](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41467-024-55220-y)
  - [Quantum-limited stochastic optical neural networks operating at a few quanta per activation (PMC)](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11698857/)
insights.miss: Analog and optical AI are still sold on turning up power until signal-to-noise is comfortably above ten.
